article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down specific errors across multi-step agent trajectories, helps isolate decisive error steps and understand reasoning limits. [2]

Researchers looked into hybrid architectures for autonomous problem formulation, noting that autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [3]

When examining high-stakes scenarios, analysts found that strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [4]

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.
article.lede: Our computer workers are investigating how independent systems balance strict instructions with the need to adapt when situations change unexpectedly.
article.lens: We look at how computational systems process complex rules and unexpected changes by reviewing current research papers and technical frameworks.
article.title: Tracing How Intelligent Systems Handle Unexpected Choices and Rules

Investigations into preference formation show that cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions and information in real-time. [5]

Studies on human-computer interaction also highlight that AI-driven training recommendation reliance correlates with reduced self-regulation and increased decision hesitation in athletes, pointing to a serial causal chain where outsourcing body signals leads to reduced autonomy. [6]

Work on foundational assumptions indicates that general preference oracle formulations provide a rigorous basis for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [7]

Additional memory studies suggest that episodic memory recall provides temporal credit assignment structures that stabilize preference formation in sequential decision tasks. [8]

Exploring curiosity, teams noted that curiosity arousal mechanisms dynamically guide exploratory behavior and shape emergent agent preferences. [9]

To handle multiple conflicting goals, systems utilize Pareto-Conditioned Proximal Policy Optimization, which means an optimization method that enables agents to learn portfolios of non-dominated policies, facilitating dynamic objective prioritization. [10]

Furthermore, value system learning from demonstrations in multi-agent reinforcement learning can leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [11]

Finally, computational creativity frameworks depend upon a structured decomposition of problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.

Decisions Already Made
Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
Abstract
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-
ment it is made; the action it commits to is la-
tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We
therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci-
sion validity and a decision ledger that realises
it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh-
ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence
guarantees at action time, placing the remain-
ing risk in information published afterwards.
Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities:
routing, which delivers that information to af-
fected decisions before their revision deadlines,
and temporal judgment, which reads it for the
time of action. The ledger is persistent state
holding each decision’s times, evidence and
background knowledge, indexed by watch con-
ditions written at decision time. Controlled
decision streams with exact labels confirm four
predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron-
tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the
accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de-
cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows
routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing
reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect
dependencies at low exposure; and the remain-
ing errors concern when a change takes effect.
Freshness makes a decision right when it is
made; routing and temporal judgment keep it
right when it is carried out.

plies without power; the Gorran substation supplies
the Bellhaven district (Figure 1). The choice was
right at 13:05 and is wrong at 20:30. The informa-
tion that settles it appeared after the decision and
refers to the restaurant only through the substation

Freshness is necessary for LLM decision-making
and insufficient on its own. A decision is judged
when it is carried out, the freshness ceiling bounds

recall follows what the ledger indexes, misleading

Limitations
Controlled streams.The decision streams are
synthetic by design: exact control over timing, ref-
erence and labels is what lets each prediction be
tested in isolation. Real news is longer and nois-
ier, dependencies can be implicit, and relevance
can be uncertain, so the magnitudes we report be-
long to these streams while the predictions concern
mechanisms. Testing the theory on logged agent
decisions, and in languages beyond English, is the
next step.
Scope of the theory.The theory models a deci-
sion as a choice among options with one revision
deadline and a binary outcome, and the freshness
ceiling assumes a constant hazard rate. Real com-
mitments are staged, partly reversible and graded
in utility, and facts change in bursts. The factori-
sation of Eq. 3 carries over, because information
must reach a decision before it can change it, but
its terms then depend on time and on the cost of
revising.
Reach of the ledger.Routing recall is bounded
by the dependencies the ledger records at decision
time, and the ledger treats routed news as trustwor-
thy. Discovering dependencies after the decision
and weighing the credibility of sources extend the
ledger beyond this paper.
Ethics Statement
The decision streams use fictional entities and con-
tain no personal data, and hosted models were
queried on this synthetic data only. Systems that
revise decisions on a user’s behalf can act on false
or adversarial news; routing should be paired with
source verification and, for consequential decisions,
with user confirmation.

/a.sc/b.sc/s.sc/t.sc/r.sc/a.sc/c.sc/t.sc
Reaching some form of consensus is often necessary for autonomous
agents that want to coordinate their actions or otherwise engage in
joint activities. One way to reach a consensus is by aggregating individ-
ual information, such as decisions, beliefs, preferences and constraints.
Judgment aggregation is a social choice method, which generalises vot-
ing, that studies the aggregation of individual judgments regarding the
truth-value of logically related propositions. As such, judgment aggre-
gation is applicable for consensus reaching problems in multi agent
systems. As other social choice theory, judgment aggregation research
is abundant with impossibility results. However, the aim of this tuto-
rial is to give an introduction to the methods of judgment aggregation,
not the impossibility results. In particular, the tutorial will introduce
the basic frameworks that model judgment aggregation problems and
give an overview of the judgment aggregation functions so far devel-
oped as well as their social theoretic and computational complexity
properties. The focus of the tutorial are consensus reaching problems
in multi agent systems that can be modelled as judgment aggregation
problems. The desirable properties of a judgment aggregation method
applied to these problems are not necessarily the same as properties
desirable in legal or political contexts, which is considered to be the

ipants are expected to be able to read and understand judgment ag-
